title: Math Reasoning in LLMs is Organized by Approach, Not Topic
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 22 Sep 2026]
    Title:Math Reasoning in LLMs is Organized by Approach, Not Topic
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Mathematical reasoning benchmarks are typically organized by topic, but language models may organize their internal computation by reusable reasoning approach instead. In this paper, we investigate whether open math-capable LLMs organize internally by topical sub-skill or by reasoning approach, and we present evidence that the approach is the key. We introduce a generation-replay protocol: a model first generates a solution, after which we replay the exact prompt-plus-generation trajectory and extract activation-importance signatures over the reasoning tokens. We cluster these signatures without supervision across eight models and five mathematical reasoning sources, then evaluate the recovered structure with structural, semantic, and intervention tests. Across all 40 model-source cells, the recovered clusters outperform matched-size random baselines. Two independent frontier-LLM judges find approach-level coherence in 77-82% of real clusters versus 6-11% in within-source controls, and topic-pure clusters usually receive labels finer than the topic itself. In approach-controlled prompting, changing the requested reasoning approach shifts cluster assignment in seven of eight model conditions, whereas paraphrases largely preserve it. These results indicate that math-capable LLMs organize internal mathematical computation by reasoning approach rather than benchmark topic. The implication is that topic-stratified benchmarks and topic-balanced training corpora can still miss the axis that matters: even deliberately topic-balanced corpora may remain imbalanced over reasoning approaches.

report.summary: New evidence suggests math-capable LLMs internally organize reasoning by reusable approach, not benchmark topic, challenging topic-based evaluation and training data design.
report.background: Mathematical reasoning benchmarks such as GSM8K and MATH are conventionally organized by topic: algebra, geometry, number theory, combinatorics. Training corpora are often balanced along the same axis, under the assumption that topical coverage equals skill coverage. But solving a math problem draws on reusable procedures—induction, contradiction, casework, substitution, constructive proof—that cut across topics. Prior interpretability work has found structured internal features and circuits, but little work tested whether math LLMs internally cluster by school subject or by method. This paper asks whether open math-capable models organize internal computation by topical sub-skill or reasoning approach. Using a generation-replay protocol, it extracts activation-importance signatures over reasoning tokens and clusters them without supervision across eight models and five math reasoning sources. The finding matters because topic-balanced benchmarks and corpora may hide uneven coverage of the approaches models actually rely on.
key_points: The paper introduces a generation-replay protocol. A model first solves a problem, then researchers replay the exact prompt-plus-generation trajectory and extract activation-importance signatures over reasoning tokens. They cluster these signatures without supervision across eight models and five mathematical reasoning sources, yielding 40 model-source cells. Recovered clusters beat matched-size random baselines in every cell, showing the structure is real rather than noise.

Independent frontier-LLM judges found approach-level coherence in 77–82% of real clusters, versus only 6–11% in within-source controls. Clusters that looked topic-pure usually received labels finer than the topic itself. This suggests the model’s internal math computation is better described by reusable reasoning approaches—such as casework or contradiction—than by benchmark categories like algebra or geometry.

Intervention tests support a causal role. When prompts controlled the requested reasoning approach, cluster assignment shifted in seven of eight model conditions. By contrast, paraphrasing the problem largely preserved cluster assignment. The clusters therefore track the method used, not surface wording, problem phrasing, or accidental lexical cues.

The result challenges an implicit assumption in data curation: balancing topics does not guarantee balanced reasoning approaches. Topic-stratified benchmarks may overstate or miss capabilities, and a corpus balanced by topic can still be skewed toward a few approaches. Evaluation and training may need to measure approach coverage directly.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this shifts evaluation and data strategy. Benchmark builders should report approach coverage—induction, contradiction, casework—alongside topic tags, because topic-balanced tests can miss systematic gaps. Training teams may need to balance or augment corpora by reasoning method, not just subject, to improve generalization and robustness. For developers, interpretability tools that recover activation structure can guide prompt design, fine-tuning mixtures, and model debugging; approach-controlled prompting already shows steerability. For regular users, the benefit is less visible but important: math assistants could become more reliable across unfamiliar problem types if models are trained and evaluated on the reasoning approaches that matter, rather than on superficial topic labels. It may also reduce brittle failures that appear when a problem is paraphrased.
report.tools: To follow up, explore interpretability libraries such as TransformerLens, nnsight, SAELens, and Captum for activation attribution and clustering. Math reasoning benchmarks and datasets include GSM8K, MATH, ProofNet, MiniF2F, and Lean-based proof corpora. Hugging Face hosts many open math-capable models for replication. For judging cluster coherence, frontier LLM APIs or open judges like Prometheus can be used. These tools let researchers test whether their own models organize computation by approach or topic.
